solution.concept_anchor: Governor-General of Bengal — title and jurisdiction 1773
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students who know Warren Hastings was 'Governor-General' assume his authority extended over all presidencies, conflating the 1773 title with the pan-India authority granted only by the Charter Act of 1833.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — The Governor-General title came from the 1773 Act itself; Hastings held the earlier designation of Governor of Bengal before this Act elevated him.
Eliminate option (c) — General administrative superintendence over Bombay and Madras was NOT granted in 1773; authority over them was restricted to matters of war, peace, and treaties only.
Eliminate option (d) — 'Governor-General of India' as a pan-India designation came with the Charter Act of 1833, not 1773.
Confirm option (b) — The 1773 Act gave the Governor-General-in-Council full supervisory authority over Bengal's civil, military, and revenue affairs, which is accurately and narrowly stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students conflate the 1773 designation with the Charter Act of 1833 title. Warren Hastings was 'Governor-General of Bengal' — not of India. His supervisory authority over Bombay and Madras was confined to war, peace, and treaties. Any option suggesting he held general administrative control over all presidencies exploits the widespread assumption that being the first Governor-General meant pan-India supremacy, which is historically incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 created the office of Governor-General for the Bengal Presidency and elevated Warren Hastings to this position. However, the title and jurisdiction were carefully circumscribed.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Hastings already held the designation of Governor of Bengal from 1772; the 1773 Act renamed and upgraded the position but did not create him anew as a simple 'Governor'.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Governor-General had full authority over Bengal's civil, military, and revenue affairs — this is an accurate, limited description.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: General administrative authority over Bombay and Madras was not granted. Superintendence was limited to matters of war, peace, and treaties — an important legal distinction.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Governor-General of India' with pan-India authority was a creation of the Charter Act of 1833, under which Lord William Bentinck became the first to hold that title.

Value Addition:
• The 1773 Act's Governor-General had only a casting vote in his Council — not a veto — making him structurally weak.
• The 1786 amendment to Pitt's India Act gave the Governor-General override powers over his Council.
• Charter Act 1833 also abolished Bombay and Madras's legislative powers, concentrating them in Calcutta.

solution.concept_anchor: 1773 Act — regulation vs. direct Crown control distinction

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 was the first instance of Parliament asserting its authority over the civil and military affairs of the East India Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act is historically recognized as the first assertion of Parliamentary supremacy over the Company's governance, breaking the immunity of a private chartered company from state oversight.

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 established direct Crown control over Indian administration by creating a Board of Control to supervise the Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The Board of Control was created by Pitt's India Act 1784, not by the 1773 Act. The 1773 Act regulated the Company but did not establish direct Crown control — that came eleven years later.

statement_analysis.statement: The Select Committee and Secret Committee reports of 1772–73 provided the parliamentary basis for the legislative intervention that resulted in the 1773 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Committees led by figures such as Burgoyne examined the Company's affairs and produced reports that substantiated Parliament's claim to regulate the Company, forming the evidentiary foundation for the Act.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (1 and 2 only) is the strongest distractor because students correctly identify Statement 1 as true but also accept Statement 2, not realizing the Board of Control was a creation of 1784, not 1773.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — The 1773 Act is universally acknowledged as the first parliamentary assertion over Company affairs; mark it Correct.
Test Statement 2 carefully — The Board of Control is definitively associated with Pitt's India Act 1784; the 1773 Act did not create any such body, making Statement 2 Incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — Parliamentary committee reports by Burgoyne and others (1772–73) are documented as the basis for legislative intervention; mark it Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in Statement 2. The phrase 'Board of Control' is strongly associated with Parliamentary control over India, and students who know this association but are not precise about dates will attribute it to the 1773 Act. In reality, the 1773 Act could only observe Company correspondence — it had no override mechanism. The Board of Control that gave Parliament active power over Indian governance came only with Pitt's India Act of 1784. This is a classic temporal-swap trap embedded in a plausible-sounding statement.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 is a landmark in the evolution of British parliamentary control over Indian governance, but its nature and limits must be precisely understood.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Act marked the first time Parliament legislated to regulate the internal affairs of a private chartered company, asserting a public interest in the governance of a territory held nominally by a trading corporation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Board of Control — a six-member body empowered to superintend, direct, and control the Company's civil, military, and revenue affairs — was established by Pitt's India Act of 1784, not by the 1773 Act. The 1773 Act only gave Parliament the right to receive Company correspondence, not to intervene in decisions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Select Committee (under Burgoyne) and Secret Committee produced detailed reports in 1772–73 exposing the Company's financial mismanagement and administrative failures, giving Parliament the political and legal justification to act.

Value Addition:
• The 1773 Act 'regulated' the Company; the 1784 Act 'controlled' it — this one-liner distinction is high-yield for both Prelims and Mains.
• The Act is sometimes called 'the first written constitution for India' in a broad sense.
• Lord North's government introduced the Act as a political compromise — not as a principled reform.

solution.concept_anchor: Court of Directors reform — tenure and rotation 1773

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 abolished the Court of Directors and replaced it with a newly constituted Board of Control.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act reformed the Court of Directors by changing tenure arrangements — it did not abolish it. The Board of Control was a creation of Pitt's India Act 1784.

statement_analysis.statement: Before 1773, Directors were elected annually by the Court of Proprietors with no restriction on the number of consecutive terms they could serve.
statement_analysis.reason: The pre-1773 structure had 24 Directors elected annually without tenure restrictions, contributing to instability and short-termism in administration.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 1773 reforms, Directors were given a four-year term, with one-fourth retiring each year on a rotational basis to ensure administrative continuity.
statement_analysis.reason: This rotational system was specifically designed to prevent short-termism and maintain institutional memory within the Court of Directors.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (1 only) tempts students who recognise Statement 1 is wrong, but they must also confirm Statements 2 and 3 are correct, which requires precise knowledge of the pre- and post-1773 structures.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — The Court of Directors was NOT abolished in 1773; it was reformed. The Board of Control came in 1784. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — The pre-1773 annual election system with no tenure cap is a documented historical fact; Statement 2 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — The four-year term with one-quarter rotating annually is the precise reform introduced by the 1773 Act; Statement 3 is Correct.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect; the answer asking for which is NOT correct is option (a) — 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 is a classic entity-swap. The abolition of the Court of Directors and creation of the Board of Control are features of Pitt's India Act 1784. Students who know that Parliamentary control increased after 1773 often erroneously project the 1784 institutional changes backward onto 1773. The 1773 Act retained the Court of Directors but restricted it — abolition came a full decade later.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 modified the structure of the Court of Directors significantly but did not dismantle it.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Court of Directors was not abolished. It continued to exist and remained the Company's governing board. The Board of Control — a separate Crown-appointed body with power to superintend the Company — was a creation of Pitt's India Act 1784.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Prior to 1773, the 24 Directors were elected annually by shareholders (Court of Proprietors) without term limits, enabling factional capture and administrative instability.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 1773 Act introduced a four-year term with staggered retirement (six Directors rotating out annually), designed to ensure experienced Directors always remained on the board.

Value Addition:
• The Court of Proprietors (shareholders) retained power to review Directors' decisions — creating an internal check within Company governance.
• Pitt's India Act 1784 finally subordinated the Court of Directors to the Crown-appointed Board of Control.
• The 1773 reforms to the Court of Directors are analogous in spirit to modern corporate governance principles of staggered board renewal.

solution.concept_anchor: Shareholder voting reform — £1,000 qualification threshold

statement_analysis.statement: Before 1773, a shareholding of £500 entitled a proprietor to vote in the Court of Proprietors.
statement_analysis.reason: The pre-1773 threshold was £500, which was easily circumvented through temporary share transfers and splitting, enabling vote manipulation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act raised the voting qualification to £1,000 held continuously for at least one year.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act raised the threshold to £1,000 held for at least one year specifically to prevent speculators from acquiring temporary shares to manipulate votes.

statement_analysis.statement: The rationale for raising the qualification threshold was to increase the Company's share capital and attract institutional investors.
statement_analysis.reason: The purpose was to reduce speculative vote-buying by small shareholders, not to raise capital. The reform was a governance measure, not a financial one.

statement_analysis.statement: The raising of voting qualification is historically significant as an early legislative attempt to link property ownership with participation in governance.
statement_analysis.reason: This reform prefigures the property-based suffrage debates of the 19th century and represents an early example of qualification-based democratic participation.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct but mistakenly assume Statement 3 also has some financial rationale basis, leading them to count all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — The £500 threshold is documented historical fact; mark Correct.
Confirm Statement 2 — The £1,000 minimum held for one year is the precise reform; mark Correct.
Test Statement 3 carefully — The Act's rationale was anti-speculation in voting, not capital mobilisation; mark Incorrect.

Confirm Statement 4 — Linking property to governance participation is a valid historical interpretation; mark Correct. Three statements are correct: answer is option (b) Only two — wait, re-check: Statements 1, 2, 4 are Correct = Only three → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap. It attributes a plausible-sounding financial rationale — attracting institutional investors — to what was a purely political governance reform. Students with only surface knowledge of the Act may accept this framing because the Company was indeed facing financial difficulties in 1773. The actual purpose was to prevent vote manipulation through temporary share purchases, a practice that had allowed factional interests to dominate shareholders' meetings.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 addressed a significant governance problem in the Court of Proprietors (the Company's shareholders' assembly): wealthy speculators were purchasing £500 shares temporarily before votes and selling them afterward, effectively buying influence over Company decisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The pre-1773 voting threshold was £500, easily exploited through share splitting and temporary transfers.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Act raised the threshold to £1,000 held continuously for at least one year, making temporary vote-buying significantly harder.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The purpose was exclusively to clean up voting practices, not to raise capital. The Act had no provision aimed at attracting institutional investors as a financial objective.
• Statement 4 — Correct: This reform is an early instance of property-based qualification for participation in institutional governance — a concept that would recur in debates about democratic franchise through the 19th century.

Value Addition:
• The Court of Proprietors could refer back Directors' decisions — a residual check on management that the Act preserved.
• The £1,000 threshold is analogous to the property qualifications that dominated British electoral reform debates before 1832.
• Share manipulation in joint-stock companies was a widespread 18th-century problem, not unique to the EIC.

solution.concept_anchor: Supreme Court Calcutta — composition, authority, and jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps the appointing authority for judges from Crown to Company, which feels plausible because the Company was the governing power in Bengal; many students assume the Company must have appointed the judges.
elimination_logic: Fix anchor pair A — The Supreme Court was established at Fort William, Calcutta, and operationalized by Letters Patent of 1774; A matches with 2.
Fix anchor pair B — The Chief Justice and three puisne judges were appointed by the Crown, not the Company; B matches with 4.
Resolve trap pair C — Jurisdiction covered British subjects in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa; C matches with 1.
By elimination, D (the imminent necessity exception) relates to Bombay and Madras's conditional subordination, not the Supreme Court; D matches with 3 — confirming option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous distractor swaps the appointing authority in pair B. Students know that the Company administered Bengal and instinctively assume it appointed judges. In reality, the Crown appointed all Supreme Court judges — a deliberate design choice creating dual sovereignty on the same territory: Company administrative power alongside Crown judicial power. This dual sovereignty was the structural source of subsequent judicial-executive conflicts.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court at Calcutta, established by the Regulating Act 1773 and operationalized by the Letters Patent of 1774, introduced several institutionally significant features that UPSC tests with precision.

Correct pairings:
• A — 2: The Supreme Court was established at Fort William (Calcutta), making it the first such court in India.
• B — 4: All judges, including the Chief Justice, were appointed by the Crown — not the Company — creating a jurisdictional duality on Company-administered territory.
• C — 1: The court's jurisdiction extended over British subjects residing in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, and over Company servants for official acts.
• D — 3: The 'imminent necessity' exception applied to the subordination of Bombay and Madras to the Governor-General-in-Council in matters of war and peace — a separate provision often confused with the Supreme Court's jurisdictional limits.

The trap pairing is B — students assign appointment power to the Company because it was the governing authority; the Crown's judicial appointment was a deliberate countervailing power.

Value Addition:
• The 1781 Amending Act corrected the Supreme Court's overreach by excluding revenue matters and non-Company Indians from its jurisdiction.
• The Nand Kumar hanging (1775) arose from the court applying English criminal law to an Indian subject — a direct consequence of the Act's ambiguous jurisdiction.
• The Chief Justice's salary was paid from Indian revenues, creating an awkward accountability question.

solution.concept_anchor: Governor-General casting vote — structural weakness of 1773 Council
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is the strongest distractor because students who know both facts (casting vote AND governance paralysis) naturally assume one caused the other, without examining whether the casting vote is actually the correct explanation of the paralysis or merely a related feature.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Warren Hastings was indeed regularly outvoted by the Clavering-Monson-Francis bloc; A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — The four Council members were appointed by the Crown, not the Company; this is a verified historical fact; R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — The governance paralysis was caused by the majority-rule structure where the Governor-General had only a casting vote (used only in ties), not by who appointed the councillors. Hostility existed because the bloc was ideologically opposed to Hastings. The appointment authority (Crown vs. Company) did not itself cause the majority opposition. R is true but does not explain A.
Conclusion: A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b). Re-check: option (b) states both correct, R not the explanation — confirm answer is b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits a reversed-causation trap. Students correctly identify both A and R as true — Hastings was outvoted, and the Council was Crown-appointed — and jump to option (a). But the causal link is missing: the paralysis arose from the structural majority-rule mechanism (Governor-General had only a casting vote in ties, not a veto), not from the fact that the Crown rather than the Company made the appointments. The appointment authority is a factually independent feature. This is a classic UPSC assertion-reason trap where two true facts are not causally connected.
solution.final_explanation:
The Council of Four created under the 1773 Act was structurally designed for collective governance, but it produced paralyzing deadlock during Hastings's tenure.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The Clavering-Monson-Francis bloc consistently outvoted Hastings on major policy matters between 1774 and 1776. The Governor-General held only a casting vote (relevant only when votes were tied 2-2), not a veto. A hostile majority of three could override him on any substantive question.

Reason (R) — Correct: The four Councillors — Clavering, Monson, Barwell, and Francis — were indeed appointed by the Crown, not by the Company. This was deliberate: Parliament wanted its nominees, not Company loyalists, to check the Governor-General.

Causal link — Absent: The governance paralysis was caused by the majority-rule decision-making structure, not by the appointment mechanism. Crown appointment ensured independent councillors, but the deadlock arose because three of the four were ideologically hostile to Hastings. Even if the Company had appointed them, a hostile majority would produce the same paralysis. R explains the source of councillors, not the source of conflict.

Value Addition:
• The 1786 amendment to Pitt's India Act gave the Governor-General override powers over his Council in specific circumstances, addressing this structural defect.
• Philip Francis (of the hostile bloc) is believed by many historians to be the author of the Letters of Junius.
• Barwell was the only Councillor who consistently supported Hastings.

solution.concept_anchor: Legislative sequence — 1773 to 1784 parliamentary control chain
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places the Amending Act of 1781 after Pitt's India Act 1784, which students who know only that 1784 'corrected' 1773 may accept, unaware that the 1781 Act was an intermediate corrective measure.
elimination_logic: Fix the starting point — The Regulating Act 1773 is definitively the first; any option not starting with it is wrong.
Identify the intermediate Act — The Amending Act (Act of Settlement) 1781 corrected jurisdictional conflicts arising from the 1773 Act; it must come before 1784.
Confirm the endpoint — Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control and is the final major reform in this sequence.
The correct order is 1773 → 1781 → 1784; option (b) reflects this sequence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who memorise the 1773–1784 pairing as 'problem and solution' frequently forget the intermediate 1781 Amending Act, which was specifically designed to address the Supreme Court's jurisdictional overreach. Options placing 1781 after 1784 exploit this gap in chronological awareness. The 1781 Act came directly in response to the Patna Case and Kasijora Case conflicts — events that arose within years of the 1773 Act — making it an earlier intervention than Pitt's comprehensive reform.
solution.final_explanation:
The regulatory evolution of British India's governance from the Regulating Act to Pitt's India Act followed a clearly sequenced legislative chain, with intermediate corrective legislation.

Correct sequence: Regulating Act 1773 → Amending Act (Act of Settlement) 1781 → Pitt's India Act 1784

• 1773: The Regulating Act created the Supreme Court and the Governor-General-in-Council but left jurisdictional boundaries ambiguous.
• 1781: The Amending Act directly responded to the Patna and Kasijora Case conflicts by limiting the Supreme Court's jurisdiction — excluding revenue matters and non-Company Indians. This is the first corrective amendment to the 1773 framework.
• 1784: Pitt's India Act created the Board of Control, giving Parliament active power to direct Company affairs, and subsequently gave the Governor-General override powers (1786 amendment).

Why wrong options fail:
• Options placing 1781 after 1784 are chronologically impossible — the jurisdictional crisis erupted immediately after 1774 and was legislatively addressed in 1781, years before Pitt's reform.
• Options omitting 1781 conflate the 1773 defects with their remedies.

Value Addition:
• The 1773–1781–1784 chain is the foundational sequence of British India's constitutional development.
• The Nand Kumar affair (1775) was a direct product of the 1773 Act's ambiguity — it predates the 1781 correction.
• Charter Act 1813 and 1833 are the next major landmarks after 1784.

solution.concept_anchor: Imminent necessity exception — subordination limits of 1773
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (the action was illegal) is the strongest distractor because students who know Bombay required Bengal's sanction for war will assume any independent action was unlawful, forgetting the 'imminent necessity' exception in the Act.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule — The 1773 Act prohibited Bombay and Madras from declaring war or making peace without the Governor-General-in-Council's sanction, EXCEPT in cases of sudden and imminent necessity.
Apply the exception to the scenario — The scenario presents an attack without warning, which falls squarely within the 'sudden and imminent necessity' exception.
Eliminate option (a) — Bombay's action was not categorically illegal; the imminent necessity exception exists precisely for such situations.
Eliminate option (b) — The 1773 Act did not give Bombay complete autonomy in all military matters; it retained subordination as the default rule.

Eliminate option (c) — Approval from the Court of Directors was not the specified mechanism; the Act required Bengal's prior sanction except in emergencies. Option (d) correctly identifies the exception as applicable.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits a scope-extension error. Students learn the rule that Bombay and Madras needed Bengal's prior sanction for war and apply it absolutely, ignoring the qualifying exception. The 'imminent necessity' clause was a deliberate recognition that real-world military emergencies do not wait for bureaucratic clearance. This exception was widely criticised because it was exploited by presidencies to bypass Bengal's authority even in non-emergency situations, but in the scenario presented, the exception applies legitimately.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 established Bengal's precedence over Bombay and Madras but built in a safety valve for genuine military emergencies.

Applicable principle: Under the 1773 Act, the Governors of Bombay and Madras could not declare war, make peace, or enter treaties with Indian powers without the prior sanction of the Governor-General-in-Council in Bengal. However, an exception existed for cases of 'sudden and imminent necessity' — where obtaining prior approval was physically impossible.

Applied to the scenario:
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Bombay's action is not automatically illegal. The sudden night attack without warning is precisely the kind of imminent necessity the Act's exception was designed to accommodate.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Bombay did not have general military autonomy; subordination was the default rule, with the exception carved out only for genuine emergencies.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The mechanism for sanction was the Governor-General-in-Council in Bengal, not the Court of Directors in London. Retroactive approval by the Court of Directors was not the specified procedure.
• Option (d) — Correct: The 'sudden and imminent necessity' exception under the 1773 Act permits Bombay's independent defensive response in this scenario.

Value Addition:
• The imminent necessity loophole was frequently abused by presidencies to conduct offensive wars without Bengal's approval.
• The Anglo-Maratha Wars saw repeated disputes about whether Bengal had properly sanctioned Bombay's military actions.
• Pitt's India Act 1784 explicitly condemned 'wars of aggression' against Indian powers — partly responding to presidency overreach.

solution.strong_distractor: b — The Kasijora Case is a strong distractor because it directly involved the Supreme Court's attempt to arrest a zamindar, which sounds like it could involve revenue administration — students may confuse it with the revenue jurisdiction settled by the 1781 Act rather than the original 1773 conflict.

Test option (c) — The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was Cornwallis's zamindari revenue reform, enacted two decades after 1773 under a different legal framework; it does NOT fit as a conflict arising from the 1773 Act.
Test option (d) — The Nand Kumar affair (1775) was a direct judicial-executive conflict arising from the 1773 Act's ambiguities; it fits. Option (c) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 mentions zamindars — the same group involved in the Kasijora Case — creating a conflation trap. Students who know all four items involve colonial administration and zamindars may not recognise that the Permanent Settlement is a distinct revenue policy reform from the 1790s, not a jurisdictional conflict arising from the 1773 Act. The three genuine conflicts (Patna Case, Kasijora Case, Nand Kumar affair) all exposed the 1773 Act's structural ambiguities and were corrected through the 1781 Amending Act or later reforms.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the four items are direct legal or constitutional conflicts arising from the Regulating Act 1773's jurisdictional ambiguities. One is a later revenue policy reform from a different era.

• Option (a) — Patna Case (1777–79): The Supreme Court asserted jurisdiction over Indians under Company revenue administration, threatening the zamindari revenue base. This is a core 1773-era conflict.
• Option (b) — Kasijora Case: The Supreme Court attempted to arrest a Bengali zamindar for debt, directly confronting the Governor-General-in-Council's revenue authority. A defining 1773-era conflict.
• Option (c) — Permanent Settlement of 1793: This was Lord Cornwallis's landmark revenue reform that fixed zamindars' land revenue in perpetuity. It was enacted under the Charter Act framework, not as a consequence of 1773 jurisdictional conflicts. This is the odd one out.
• Option (d) — Nand Kumar affair (1775): The Supreme Court's application of English criminal law to an Indian subject, exposing the 1773 Act's failure to delineate personal jurisdiction. A defining 1773-era crisis.

Value Addition:
• The 1781 Amending Act directly addressed the Patna and Kasijora conflicts by limiting Supreme Court jurisdiction.
• The Permanent Settlement fixed revenue demand but entrenched zamindars as permanent landowners — a long-term consequence unrelated to 1773 jurisdictional disputes.
• Nand Kumar was hanged under English law for forgery — a crime that did not carry capital punishment under Mughal legal tradition.

solution.concept_anchor: Correspondence disclosure — observation without override power in 1773

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 required the East India Company to submit its civil, military, and revenue correspondence from India to the Secretary of State and the Treasury, but the government had no formal power to reject or override Company decisions on the basis of this correspondence.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1773 Act created a disclosure obligation but no intervention mechanism — the government could observe but not control. Active override power came only with Pitt's India Act 1784.

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 similarly confined the Board of Control to receiving Company correspondence without the authority to issue binding directions to the Court of Directors.
statement_analysis.reason: The Board of Control created by the 1784 Act had active power to superintend, direct, and control all Company affairs — it could issue binding directions, unlike the passive oversight role under the 1773 Act.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is the strongest distractor because students who know both the 1773 Act and the 1784 Act involved government oversight of Company correspondence may assume both had similar passive roles, not recognising the fundamental shift in power from observation to control.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — The 1773 Act's disclosure requirement without override authority is a documented historical limitation; Statement 1 is Correct.
Test Statement 2 — The Board of Control under Pitt's 1784 Act had active superintendence and directive powers over the Company, not passive receipt of correspondence; Statement 2 is Incorrect.
The relationship is: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the language of 'receiving correspondence' — which sounds similar to the 1773 arrangement — to suggest the 1784 Act was equally passive. This exploits the assumption that reforms are gradual and similar in nature. In reality, the Board of Control represented a qualitative leap: from a government that could observe to a government that could command. The 1773 Act gave the government a reading right; the 1784 Act gave it a governing right.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between the 1773 and 1784 oversight mechanisms is one of the most tested conceptual contrasts in this period.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 1773 Act required the Company to lay before the Secretary of State and Treasury all correspondence on civil, military, and revenue matters. However, this was a transparency measure only — the government had no statutory authority to refuse, modify, or override Company decisions based on what it read. It was 'observation without teeth.'
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Board of Control established by Pitt's India Act 1784 was not a passive recipient of correspondence. It had the power to superintend, direct, and control all acts, operations, and concerns of the Company relating to civil, military, and revenue affairs. It could issue secret orders that even the Directors could not challenge on certain matters.

Value Addition:
• The one-liner distinction: '1773 regulated the Company; 1784 controlled it.'
• The Secret Committee of three Directors under Board supervision (1784) replaced the leaky Court of Proprietors on sensitive intelligence matters.
• The 1773 disclosure mechanism is considered the first formal accountability mechanism in the governance of British India.

solution.concept_anchor: Statutory prohibition on gifts and private trade — 1773 Act
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Pitt's India Act 1784) is a strong distractor because students associate the major anti-corruption institutional reforms with 1784, and may assume the statutory gift prohibition also came at that stage rather than in 1773.
elimination_logic: Identify the event being described — The statutory prohibition on Company servants accepting gifts or engaging in private trade with penalties of forfeiture and imprisonment.
Recall that Clive's administrative attempt to ban gifts in 1765 preceded this — the statutory backing came from the 1773 Act.
Eliminate option (c) — Pitt's 1784 Act addressed oversight and the Board of Control, not the personal conduct prohibition with statutory penalties.

Eliminate options (b) and (d) — The Dual Government system (1765) was Clive's administrative arrangement and carried no statutory force; the Charter Act 1793 dealt with trade monopoly extension, not gift prohibitions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students know Clive attempted administrative reforms in 1765 and associate corruption control with Pitt's comprehensive 1784 reforms. The fact that the Regulating Act 1773 itself carried the first statutory prohibition on gifts and private trade — with enforceable penalties — is a less-recalled detail. The trap places 'Pitt's India Act 1784' as an option to exploit the assumption that meaningful anti-corruption law came only with the more comprehensive 1784 Act.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 was the first legislation to give statutory force to the prohibition on Company servants engaging in private trade or accepting gifts from Indian rulers and merchants.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Regulating Act 1773 explicitly prohibited gift-taking and private trade by Company servants and attached penalties of forfeiture of property and imprisonment.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Clive's Dual Government arrangements of 1765 were administrative orders without statutory force — they could not bind servants with the same legal authority.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Pitt's India Act 1784 focused on the governance structure (Board of Control, Governor-General's powers) and did not introduce the personal conduct prohibition for the first time.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Charter Act 1793 renewed the Company's monopoly and made administrative adjustments but was not the source of the gift-taking prohibition.

Value Addition:
• Despite the statutory prohibition, enforcement was weak — Hastings himself faced impeachment on corruption-related charges.
• Cornwallis (Governor-General 1786–93) addressed the enforcement gap by raising Company servants' salaries to reduce the financial incentive for corruption.
• The 1773 prohibition is considered the first parliamentary anti-corruption statute in Indian administration.

solution.concept_anchor: Nand Kumar affair — constitutional significance and legal basis
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because it correctly identifies the accusation (bribery) and the conviction (forgery) but incorrectly attributes the charge of forgery to Hastings's political enemies in the Council rather than to Hastings's allies — a subtle reversal of who initiated the charge.
elimination_logic: Test option (a) — The forgery charge was brought by Hastings's allies, not by the hostile Council bloc; the partial reversal makes this incorrect.
Test option (b) — Nand Kumar was tried for forgery, convicted under English law, and hanged. The hanging exposed the application of English capital law to an Indian subject — correctly matched.

Test option (c) — The Nand Kumar affair demonstrated the 1773 Act's failure to delineate the Supreme Court's criminal jurisdiction over Indian subjects, not its exclusive power over Company servants — overstated.
Test option (d) — The 1781 Amending Act, not the 1773 Act itself, resolved the jurisdictional ambiguity that the Nand Kumar case exposed; the 1773 Act never resolved it.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) contains a partial-truth trap: it gets the charges right (Nand Kumar accused Hastings of bribery; Nand Kumar was charged with forgery) but reverses the agency — students must know that the forgery charge was prosecuted by Hastings's supporters, not by his opponents. This is a subtle factual reversal that requires precise reading of the sequence of events rather than general familiarity with the affair.
solution.final_explanation:
The Nand Kumar affair of 1775 was the most dramatic constitutional conflict to emerge from the 1773 Act's ambiguities during Hastings's tenure.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The forgery charge against Nand Kumar was not brought by Hastings's opponents (the Clavering-Monson-Francis bloc); it was initiated by Hastings's allies before the Supreme Court — widely seen as a retaliatory move after Nand Kumar accused Hastings of bribery before the Council.
• Option (b) — Correct: Nand Kumar was tried for forgery under English law, convicted, and hanged. This exposed the critical ambiguity in the 1773 Act — whether the Supreme Court could apply English capital criminal law (which prescribed hanging for forgery) to Indian subjects. It is correctly identified as the first major judicial-executive conflict in British India.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The affair highlighted the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court over Indian subjects in criminal matters generally, not merely over Company servants in their official capacity.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 1773 Act did not resolve the jurisdictional conflict it created; resolution came only with the 1781 Amending Act, which excluded Indians not employed by the Company from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• Forgery was a capital offence under English law but not under Mughal legal traditions applicable to Indians.
• Historians debate whether the forgery charge was politically motivated — making this a case study in judicial independence.
• Philip Francis later made the Nand Kumar affair a central charge in the Hastings impeachment proceedings (1788–1795).

solution.concept_anchor: EIC financial crisis and parliamentary leverage for 1773 intervention

statement_analysis.statement: The financial bankruptcy of the East India Company and its request for a government loan of £1.4 million provided the immediate leverage that enabled Parliament to impose regulatory conditions on the Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The Company's financial distress — caused partly by maintaining armies, wars, and corrupt administration — forced it to seek a Parliamentary bailout, giving Parliament the political and legal justification to attach regulatory conditions.

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Plassey (1757) immediately prompted Parliament to pass the Regulating Act, as the scale of territorial acquisition alarmed the British government into swift legislative action.
statement_analysis.reason: Plassey occurred in 1757 and the Regulating Act came in 1773 — a gap of 16 years. Plassey expanded Company power but did not immediately prompt legislative action; the Act came after accumulated financial and administrative failures over subsequent years, particularly the Buxar victory of 1764 and the Dual Government's failures.

statement_analysis.statement: The conceptual tension between the Company's status as a 'trading corporation' and its emerging role as a 'territorial sovereign' was a central justification used by Parliament to assert its right to regulate the Company's affairs.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament's regulatory intervention was justified on the grounds that governing vast territories and populations was a public function that could not remain entirely in private hands — the Company had transformed beyond its charter identity.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (1, 2 and 3) is the strongest distractor because students who know Plassey was foundational to the expansion of Company power assume it also immediately triggered legislative action, without registering the 16-year gap.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — The £1.4 million loan request as Parliamentary leverage is a well-documented historical fact; mark Correct.
Challenge Statement 2 carefully — Plassey was 1757; the Regulating Act was 1773 — 16 years later. The word 'immediately' makes Statement 2 Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — The trading company vs. territorial sovereign conceptual tension is the doctrinal foundation of Parliamentary intervention; mark Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a scope-extension trap through the word 'immediately'. Students know Plassey is causally connected to the conditions that led to the 1773 Act — it is taught as the foundational event — and may overlook that 16 years elapsed between Plassey and the Act, with the Battle of Buxar (1764) and the Dual Government's failures (1765 onwards) being the more proximate causes. The Act addressed accumulated failures, not an immediate post-Plassey crisis.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 emerged from a confluence of military expansion, administrative failure, and financial collapse — but the causal chain is more complex than a simple Plassey-to-Act narrative.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Company's request for a government loan of £1.4 million gave Parliament its clearest constitutional opportunity: a private entity seeking public funds could not remain immune from public accountability. The loan became the leverage for regulatory conditions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'immediately' is the trap. Plassey (1757) created the conditions for territorial expansion but did not trigger immediate legislation. Parliament acted only in 1773 — after the Battle of Buxar (1764), Clive's Dual Government (1765), its administrative failures, and the Company's resulting financial crisis. Sixteen years of accumulated problems preceded the Act.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The constitutional argument that a trading company cannot be permitted to exercise sovereign functions — levying taxes, administering justice, making war and peace — without Parliamentary oversight was the doctrinal foundation of the 1773 intervention.

Value Addition:
• The Battle of Buxar (1764) is a closer proximate cause than Plassey — it gave the Company the Diwani rights that created the Dual Government.
• The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa was granted by the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II in 1765 — this is what made the Company a 'de facto sovereign'.
• Robert Clive's Dual Government separated revenue collection (Company) from administration (Nawab) — a system that failed catastrophically by the early 1770s.

solution.concept_anchor: Amending Act 1781 — jurisdictional correction for Supreme Court
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (excluded all Indians from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction entirely) is the strongest distractor because students who know the 1781 Act limited the court's reach over Indians may over-generalise and think all Indians were excluded, when in fact Company-employed Indians retained their exposure to the court.
elimination_logic: Recall the purpose of the 1781 Act — It was passed to address jurisdictional conflicts between the Supreme Court and the Council arising from the 1773 Act.
Eliminate option (a) — Abolishing the Supreme Court was never done; it continued to function and was eventually replaced by the High Court system in 1862.
Eliminate option (b) — The exclusion was not absolute; Indians directly employed by the Company remained within the court's jurisdiction for acts in that capacity.

Eliminate option (c) — Transferring criminal jurisdiction to the Council would have been a major constitutional change not supported historically; the 1781 Act dealt with revenue and civil jurisdiction, not a wholesale transfer of criminal powers.
Confirm option (d) — The 1781 Act excluded revenue matters from the court's jurisdiction and exempted Indians not directly employed by the Company from its reach — the correct characterisation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits a scope-extension trap. Students know the 1781 Act limited the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over Indians and may over-read this as a complete exclusion. The key distinction is that Indians employed by the Company for official purposes retained exposure to the court — only those not in Company employment were exempted. The exclusion was of non-Company Indians, not all Indians.
solution.final_explanation:
The Amending Act of 1781 (also called the Act of Settlement) was enacted specifically to correct the jurisdictional overreach of the Supreme Court established under the 1773 Act.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court was not abolished. It continued to function until it was replaced by the Calcutta High Court under the High Courts Act of 1861.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The exclusion was not absolute. Indians directly employed by the Company retained exposure to the Supreme Court for acts done in that official capacity. Only Indians not in Company employment were excluded from its general jurisdiction.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Criminal jurisdiction was not transferred to the Governor-General-in-Council. The 1781 Act made targeted adjustments to revenue and personal jurisdiction — it did not restructure criminal authority.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Act excluded revenue-related matters from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction (protecting zamindars from court interference with revenue collection) and exempted Indians not directly employed by the Company from its general reach.

Value Addition:
• The Patna Case and Kasijora Case directly caused the 1781 legislation — these cases involved zamindars and revenue disputes.
• The Calcutta Mayor's Court was also regulated to prevent it extending its reach to mofussil (rural) areas.
• The 1781 Act is a classic example of corrective legislation — tested by UPSC as a consequence of the 1773 Act's defects.

solution.concept_anchor: Court of Proprietors vs. Court of Directors — internal Company structure

statement_analysis.statement: The Court of Proprietors and the Court of Directors were the same body under the East India Company structure, with shareholders directly managing Company affairs.
statement_analysis.reason: They were two distinct bodies: the Court of Proprietors was the shareholders' assembly (the general meeting), while the Court of Directors was the management board. The 1773 Act preserved and defined both.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Regulating Act 1773, the Court of Proprietors retained the power to refer back or review decisions of the Court of Directors, but this power was restricted in matters of Indian revenues and military or civil governance.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act preserved the Proprietors' review power as a check on Directors, but restricted it in the sensitive domains of Indian revenues and civil-military governance to prevent shareholder interference in administrative decisions.

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 transferred all powers of the Court of Proprietors to the Court of Directors, eliminating the role of shareholders in Company governance.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act did not eliminate the Proprietors' role. It restricted their powers in specific domains but retained them as a check on Directors — the shareholders' assembly continued to function and elected Directors.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (2 only) tempts students who know Statement 2 is correct, but they must also examine Statements 1 and 3 and find both incorrect — requiring students to confirm that the question asks what is NOT correct, where both 1 and 3 qualify.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — The Court of Proprietors and Court of Directors were distinct bodies with different functions; conflating them is factually wrong — Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2 — The restricted review power of Proprietors over Directors in Indian revenue and governance matters is accurately stated — Statement 2 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — The Act restricted, not eliminated, Proprietors' powers; shareholders continued to elect Directors and retained residual review rights — Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct; answer is option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statements 1 and 3 both exploit the conflation trap — treating two distinct Company bodies as identical or suggesting one absorbed the other. Students who are unfamiliar with the internal structure of the East India Company often know only 'the Directors' as the governing body and assume shareholders played no institutional role. In reality, the Court of Proprietors was a constitutionally recognised body under the Company's charter and the 1773 Act, and the tension between shareholder democracy and professional management was a genuine institutional dynamic.
solution.final_explanation:
The East India Company had two distinct internal governance bodies, and the 1773 Act engaged with both.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Court of Proprietors was the shareholders' general assembly; the Court of Directors was the 24-member management board elected by Proprietors. They were structurally, functionally, and legally separate. Conflating them is a fundamental error.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Proprietors retained a power of review over Directors' decisions, but the 1773 Act drew a boundary — in matters of Indian revenues and civil-military governance, this review power was curtailed to prevent shareholders from interfering with administrative decisions on policy grounds.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Act did not transfer or eliminate Proprietors' powers. It imposed targeted restrictions in sensitive domains while preserving the shareholders' assembly as an institutional actor. Proprietors continued to elect Directors on the new four-year rotational basis.

Value Addition:
• This internal tension between shareholder democracy and professional governance is a recurring theme in corporate governance history.
• Pitt's India Act 1784 further subordinated both bodies to the Crown's Board of Control — reducing the internal Company tension by creating an external authority above both.
• The Court of Proprietors is analogous to a modern Annual General Meeting; the Court of Directors to a Board of Directors.

solution.concept_anchor: Pitt's India Act 1784 — corrections to specific 1773 defects

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control, giving Parliament active power to superintend and direct Company affairs — addressing the 1773 Act's limitation of observation without override authority.
statement_analysis.reason: The Board of Control was the direct institutional response to the 1773 Act's 'oversight without teeth' problem — the government could now issue binding directions, not merely receive correspondence.

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 immediately and directly granted the Governor-General a personal veto over his Council, resolving the majority-rule paralysis experienced by Warren Hastings.
statement_analysis.reason: The veto/override power for the Governor-General came through a further amendment in 1786, not directly from Pitt's 1784 Act itself. The 1784 Act addressed the Board of Control; the 1786 amendment addressed the Governor-General's Council authority.

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 replaced the leaking Court of Proprietors on sensitive intelligence matters with a Secret Committee of three Directors operating under Board of Control supervision.
statement_analysis.reason: The Secret Committee of three Directors, operating under Board supervision, was created to handle sensitive military and diplomatic communications securely — addressing the intelligence security problem of the open Court of Proprietors.

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 fully resolved the jurisdictional conflict between the Supreme Court and the Governor-General-in-Council that had emerged under the 1773 Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The jurisdictional conflict between the Supreme Court and the Council was addressed by the Amending Act of 1781, not by Pitt's 1784 Act. The 1784 Act did not specifically address the court-council jurisdictional issue.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct but also accept Statement 2 (veto power) as a feature of the 1784 Act, not recognising the critical distinction that the override power came through the 1786 amendment.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Board of Control as the solution to oversight-without-power is a core feature of the 1784 Act; mark Correct.
Challenge Statement 2 — The Governor-General override power came through the 1786 amendment, not from the 1784 Act itself; mark Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3 — Secret Committee of three Directors is an attributed feature of the 1784 Act; mark Correct.
Test Statement 4 — The Supreme Court-Council jurisdictional conflict was resolved by the 1781 Amending Act, not the 1784 Act; mark Incorrect. Two statements correct — answer is option (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the critical trap. Students who know that Pitt's India Act and subsequent amendments gave the Governor-General override powers often attribute all of these changes to the 1784 Act itself, not distinguishing between the 1784 Act and the 1786 amendment. This temporal imprecision is a classic UPSC trap: the 1784 Act restructured the oversight mechanism at the Board level; the 1786 amendment (a separate legislative act) addressed the Governor-General's personal authority within his Council.
solution.final_explanation:
Pitt's India Act 1784 was a comprehensive reform that addressed several — but not all — of the 1773 Act's defects. Precision about what each specific provision did is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Board of Control directly solved the 1773 Act's 'observation without power' problem by giving Parliament active authority to superintend and direct Company civil, military, and revenue affairs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The override/veto power for the Governor-General over his Council came through a separate 1786 amendment, not from the 1784 Act itself. The 1784 Act restructured oversight at the London level; the 1786 amendment fixed the governance problem at the Calcutta level.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Secret Committee of three Directors under Board supervision replaced the open Court of Proprietors for sensitive dispatches, addressing a genuine intelligence security vulnerability.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The court-council jurisdictional conflict had already been addressed by the 1781 Amending Act (Act of Settlement). The 1784 Act did not revisit this.

Value Addition:
• The 1784 Act introduced a dual control system: Board of Control (government) + Court of Directors (Company) — a balance that defined governance until 1858.
• Lord Cornwallis became the first Governor-General to exercise expanded Council override powers under the 1786 amendment.
• The 1858 Government of India Act finally abolished both the Court of Directors and the Board of Control, transferring power directly to the Crown.

solution.concept_anchor: Warren Hastings impeachment — rooted in 1773 governance vacuum
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is the strongest distractor because students who know both facts — Hastings was paralyzed by his Council and later impeached — naturally assume his Council difficulties directly caused the impeachment, when in reality the impeachment arose from specific acts (Rohilla War funding, Chait Singh episode) enabled by the governance vacuum, not from the Council paralysis itself.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Hastings's impeachment proceedings ran from 1788 to 1795 and were partly rooted in charges arising from his governance under the flawed 1773 framework; A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Hastings was upgraded from Governor of Bengal to Governor-General directly as a result of the 1773 Act; R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — R explains how Hastings came to hold the position, not why he was impeached. His elevation to Governor-General is a precondition for the impeachment story, not its cause. The impeachment arose from specific acts of governance, not from the fact of his elevation. R is true but does not explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct_option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This assertion-reason pair traps students who see two related true facts and assume one explains the other. The Assertion — that Hastings's impeachment was partly rooted in the 1773 framework's governance vacuum — is true in the sense that the Act's ambiguities created conditions for extra-constitutional conduct. The Reason — that he was elevated by the 1773 Act from Governor to Governor-General — is also true. But the 1773 Act's role in his elevation does not explain the impeachment. The impeachment arose from specific policy decisions (Rohilla War, Chait Singh affair, Begums of Oudh) that were enabled by the ambiguous governance framework — a more complex causal chain than the Reason captures.
solution.final_explanation:
The Hastings impeachment is a landmark event in British-Indian constitutional history that connects several threads of the 1773 Act's legacy.

Assertion (A) — Correct: Warren Hastings faced impeachment proceedings from 1788 to 1795. The charges — including corruption, the Rohilla War policy, the Chait Singh episode, and the Begums of Oudh affair — were partly enabled by the governance vacuum created by the 1773 Act, which left the Governor-General structurally weak against his Council while creating ambiguous accountability mechanisms.

Reason (R) — Correct: Hastings was serving as Governor of Bengal (appointed 1772) and was elevated to the newly created position of Governor-General directly by the 1773 Act. Without that Act, the position he held — and the authority he exercised — would not have existed.

Causal link — Absent: The 1773 Act elevated Hastings to the position, but it does not explain why he was impeached. His elevation is chronologically and logically prior to the impeachment, not its cause. The impeachment arose from specific acts of governance committed in the exercise of power — some of which were enabled by the Act's ambiguities, but the Act's creation of the position is not the explanation for those acts.

Value Addition:
• Hastings was acquitted after a seven-year trial — one of the longest impeachment proceedings in British parliamentary history.
• Edmund Burke led the prosecution; Warren Hastings spent his personal fortune defending himself.
• The impeachment debates shaped British public opinion about empire and accountability.

solution.concept_anchor: Dual sovereignty — Crown judges on Company territory

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Regulating Act 1773, the judges of the Supreme Court at Calcutta were appointed by the East India Company, since it was the governing authority in Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court judges — including the Chief Justice — were appointed by the Crown, not the Company, creating a deliberate dual sovereignty on Company-administered territory.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court's salary was paid from Indian revenues, which raised questions about whose institutional servant the Chief Justice actually was.
statement_analysis.reason: While appointed by the Crown, the Chief Justice's salary was drawn from Indian revenues collected by the Company — creating a genuine accountability ambiguity that is considered the earliest instance of separation of judicial and executive authority in Indian constitutional history.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is the strongest distractor because students who know the Supreme Court had Crown authority may also assume Crown appointment, but on reflection assume the Company — the territorial administrator — must have handled appointments. The dual authority of Crown appointment plus Company-funded salary is a counterintuitive pairing.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — Judges were appointed by the Crown, not the Company; the use of 'Company' as the appointing authority makes Statement 1 Incorrect.
Test Statement 2 — The Chief Justice's salary from Indian revenues is a documented feature that created accountability ambiguity; Statement 2 is Correct.
Statement 1 Incorrect + Statement 2 Correct → answer is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 deploys an entity-swap — substituting 'Company' for 'Crown' as the appointing authority. This feels plausible because the Company was the de facto government in Bengal and students assume that whoever governs a territory appoints its judges. The deliberate design of Crown appointment was precisely to create an independent judiciary not beholden to the Company — making the Company-salary-plus-Crown-appointment combination a genuine constitutional innovation. The salary ambiguity (Crown servant paid from Company-administered revenues) is the kind of institutional subtlety that UPSC rewards precision on.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court at Calcutta represented a pioneering institutional design: a Crown-appointed judicial body operating on Company-administered territory — the earliest separation of judicial and executive authority in British India.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Judicial appointments to the Supreme Court were made by the Crown — not the Company. This was deliberate: Parliament wanted judges independent of the Company's executive authority to check potential administrative abuses.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Chief Justice's salary was paid from Indian revenues administered by the Company, creating an ambiguous accountability structure. This tension — Crown appointment, Company-funded salary, operating on Company-administered territory — is considered the genesis of independent judicial authority in Indian constitutional history.

Value Addition:
• The first Chief Justice of the Calcutta Supreme Court was Sir Elijah Impey — a school friend of Warren Hastings, which became a controversy given his role in the Nand Kumar case.
• The High Courts Act of 1861 replaced the Supreme Court with the Calcutta High Court, abolishing the dual system.
• The model of Crown-appointed judges on Company territory is an early ancestor of the independent judiciary provisions in Part V of the Indian Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Permanent Settlement 1793 — distinct from 1773 revenue framework
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Regulating Act 1773) is the strongest distractor because the Act did give the Governor-General-in-Council authority over revenue affairs in Bengal, leading students to assume it also reformed zamindari tenure — when in fact that reform came 20 years later under Cornwallis.
elimination_logic: Identify what 'fixing land revenue demand in perpetuity' specifically refers to — this is the defining feature of the Permanent Settlement, not any general revenue authority provision.
Eliminate option (a) — The 1773 Act gave the Governor-General authority over revenue affairs but did NOT fix zamindars' revenue demand in perpetuity; that was a separate reform.
Eliminate option (b) — The 1781 Amending Act dealt with jurisdictional conflicts, not zamindari revenue reform.
Eliminate option (d) — Pitt's India Act 1784 restructured governance oversight, not zamindari revenue arrangements.
Confirm option (c) — The Permanent Settlement of 1793 under Cornwallis is the specific reform that fixed Bengal zamindars' revenue liability in perpetuity.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1773 Act gave the Governor-General-in-Council authority over 'revenue affairs', and the Kasijora Case showed that the Council became protective of zamindars against Supreme Court interference. Students may infer from this protective stance that the 1773 Act itself formalised the zamindari system — but the formalisation of zamindari tenure through fixed perpetual revenue demand is a feature of the Permanent Settlement of 1793, two full decades later under a different Governor-General.
solution.final_explanation:
The zamindari system was shaped by multiple overlapping colonial interventions, and distinguishing their specific contributions is essential.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Regulating Act 1773 gave the Governor-General-in-Council authority over Bengal's revenue affairs and created a political environment protective of zamindars (as seen in the Kasijora Case), but it did not reform or formalise zamindari tenure with any fixed revenue demand.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Amending Act 1781 excluded revenue matters from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction — protecting zamindars from court interference — but did not create any permanent revenue settlement.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Permanent Settlement of 1793, introduced by Governor-General Cornwallis, fixed the land revenue demand on Bengal zamindars in perpetuity. In exchange for paying a fixed annual sum to the Company, zamindars became hereditary proprietors of their lands.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Pitt's India Act 1784 restructured the governance framework at the Board of Control level and addressed the Governor-General's Council powers; it had no direct provision regarding zamindari revenue arrangements.

Value Addition:
• The Permanent Settlement created a class of loyal landed intermediaries — aligned with British interests — which was Cornwallis's political objective.
• The ryotwari system (Munro, Madras) and mahalwari system (North-West Provinces) were alternatives to the zamindari/Permanent Settlement model.
• The 1793 settlement locked revenue demand permanently, meaning the Company could not benefit from agricultural expansion — a major fiscal miscalculation.

solution.concept_anchor: Four structural defects of the 1773 Act — matched to their descriptions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c swaps the descriptions of the Governor-General's casting vote defect and the supervisory authority loophole, which are both about limited authority and students may conflate them.
elimination_logic: Fix anchor pair A — No demarcation between Supreme Court and Council jurisdictions is an unambiguous, well-known defect; A matches 2.
Fix anchor pair B — The Governor-General's casting vote (only in ties, no veto) making him hostage to a hostile majority; B matches 1.
Resolve pair C — Supervisory authority over Bombay and Madras was narrow, with the imminent necessity loophole; C matches 4.
By elimination D — Government receiving correspondence without power to intervene is the 'oversight without teeth' defect; D matches 3; confirming option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap pairs two 'limited authority' defects — the casting vote restriction and the narrow supervisory authority over presidencies — because both involve the Governor-General or the central authority being constrained. Students who recall that 'the Governor-General was weak' may attach the wrong specific description to each defect. Precision requires distinguishing: the casting vote is about Council decision-making; the supervisory limitation is about presidencies and contains the specific 'imminent necessity' loophole.
solution.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 had four fundamental structural defects that made it an imperfect constitutional framework, each requiring separate corrective legislation.

Correct pairings:
• A — 2: The failure to demarcate the boundary between the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and the Council's executive authority was the most immediate defect, producing the Patna Case, Kasijora Case, and Nand Kumar affair within years.
• B — 1: The Governor-General's casting vote — exercisable only in tied votes — meant the hostile Clavering-Monson-Francis bloc could consistently outvote Hastings on substantive matters, paralyzing governance.
• C — 4: Supervisory authority over Bombay and Madras was limited to war, peace, and treaties, and even that was qualified by the 'imminent necessity' exception — rendering subordination partial and exploitable.
• D — 3: The government's right to receive Company correspondence without any power to override or reject decisions gave Parliament visibility but no control — the fundamental 'oversight without teeth' problem corrected only by the Board of Control in 1784.

Value Addition:
• All four defects had specific legislative correctives: (A) → 1781 Amending Act; (B) → 1786 amendment; (C) → ongoing regulatory struggle; (D) → 1784 Pitt's Act.
• UPSC often frames defects as 'which was corrected by which Act' — a cross-referencing question type.
• The casting vote defect is unique to the 1773 Act — no other major colonial constitutional Act gave the chief executive such weak council powers.

solution.concept_anchor: First parliamentary oversight mechanism — 1773 not 1784
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Pitt's India Act 1784) is the strongest distractor because students associate 'first meaningful parliamentary control over India' with 1784, when the Board of Control was established with active governing powers — forgetting that the 1773 Act was the first assertion of Parliamentary supremacy, even if its oversight was limited.
elimination_logic: Identify what 'first assertion of Parliamentary supremacy over Company civil and military affairs' means — this is the doctrinal claim about the 1773 Act.
Eliminate option (a) — The Charter Act 1813 opened India to missionaries and modified trade monopoly; it was not the first parliamentary assertion over Company governance.
Eliminate option (c) — Pitt's India Act 1784 expanded and deepened parliamentary control but was the second major intervention, not the first.
Eliminate option (d) — The Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown — a much later development.
Confirm option (b) — The Regulating Act 1773 is universally acknowledged as the first parliamentary assertion of authority over the Company's civil and military affairs.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap here substitutes Pitt's India Act 1784 — the more famous and consequential parliamentary control measure — for the 1773 Act. Students associate 'parliamentary control over India' with the Board of Control, which was 1784, and may incorrectly attribute the 'first' claim to 1784. The 1773 Act was weaker in its oversight mechanisms, but it was temporally and doctrinally the first assertion of Parliament's right to regulate the Company's governance. UPSC frequently tests this 'first' distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
The claim of being the 'first' measure of Parliamentary oversight over the East India Company belongs exclusively to the Regulating Act of 1773.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Charter Act of 1813 renewed the Company's charter while ending its trade monopoly with India (though the China trade monopoly continued until 1833). It was a later reform in a different legislative context.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Regulating Act 1773 is the first Parliamentary legislation that asserted the right of the British state to regulate the civil and military affairs of the East India Company — breaking the immunity of a private chartered corporation from public law oversight.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Pitt's India Act 1784 was the second major Parliamentary intervention and created the more powerful Board of Control — but it built upon the precedent established by the 1773 Act, not upon nothing.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Government of India Act 1858 transferred the Company's entire governing authority to the Crown, dissolving the Company — a fundamentally different category of legislation.

Value Addition:
• The doctrinal chain: 1773 (first assertion) → 1784 (active control) → 1813/1833 (Charter renewals) → 1858 (Crown takeover) → 1919/1935 (representative government).
• UPSC tests the 'first' claim in this chain frequently — the answer is always 1773, not 1784.
• The 1773 Act is sometimes called the 'foundation stone' of British India's constitutional evolution.

solution.concept_anchor: Supreme Court Calcutta — jurisdictional limits and conflicts

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court established under the Regulating Act 1773 had jurisdiction over all Indian natives in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in both civil and criminal matters.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court did NOT have jurisdiction over Indian natives in their disputes among themselves. Its jurisdiction was over British subjects, Company servants, and — controversially — Indians working under Company authority. This limitation was the source of major constitutional conflicts.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court was established by the Regulating Act 1773, but it was operationalized only after the issuance of Letters Patent in 1774.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act authorized the Supreme Court in 1773 but the actual Letters Patent that constituted it and defined its jurisdiction were issued in 1774 — an important distinction between legislative authorization and executive operationalization.

statement_analysis.statement: The Regulating Act 1773 did not clearly demarcate the boundary between the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and the Governor-General-in-Council's executive authority, which led to immediate constitutional conflicts.
statement_analysis.reason: This structural ambiguity is universally identified as the most consequential defect of the Act, producing the Patna Case, Kasijora Case, and Nand Kumar affair within the first few years of the Supreme Court's operation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (1, 2 and 3) is the strongest distractor because students who recall the Supreme Court's broad mandate may assume it covered all persons in Bengal — missing the critical exclusion of Indian natives in inter-se disputes.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 carefully — Jurisdiction over 'all Indian natives' in all matters is an over-statement. The court explicitly lacked jurisdiction over Indian natives in their disputes among themselves; Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 2 — The distinction between the 1773 Act's authorization and the 1774 Letters Patent operationalizing the court is a documented historical fact; Statement 2 is Correct.
Confirm Statement 3 — The jurisdictional ambiguity is the Act's most well-documented structural defect; Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct; Statement 1 incorrect — answer is option (c): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 deploys the scope-extension technique by adding 'all Indian natives' and 'both civil and criminal matters' to a statement about the Supreme Court's jurisdiction. The court did have some jurisdiction over Indians (particularly those employed by the Company), and the attempt to extend this to Indian zamindars in revenue cases caused the Kasijora conflict. But blanket jurisdiction over 'all Indian natives in their disputes among themselves' was precisely what the court did NOT have — making Statement 1 a confident-sounding but factually wrong overstatement.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court at Calcutta had a carefully circumscribed jurisdiction that the 1773 Act failed to define with sufficient precision — producing an institutional crisis within years of its establishment.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court expressly lacked jurisdiction over Indian natives in disputes among themselves. Its reach extended over British subjects, Company servants for official acts, and (controversially) Indians who had entered into contracts with or worked under the Company. The attempt to extend jurisdiction beyond these categories — as in the Kasijora Case — was what created the constitutional conflict.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Regulating Act of 1773 authorised the creation of the Supreme Court, but the Letters Patent of 1774 were the executive instrument that formally constituted it, defined its seal, and established its rules of procedure. The authorisation and the operationalization were separate acts in 1773 and 1774 respectively.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The failure to demarcate boundaries between judicial and executive authority is the most consequential structural defect of the Act — producing three major conflicts (Patna Case, Kasijora Case, Nand Kumar affair) that required the 1781 Amending Act to partially resolve.

Value Addition:
• The 1781 Amending Act excluded revenue matters and non-Company Indians from the court's jurisdiction — essentially writing the boundary the 1773 Act had omitted.
• The Supreme Court consisted of one Chief Justice and three puisne judges — all appointed by the Crown.
• It was the first court in India to apply English law as a personal law to British subjects.
